- Do not use when high-frequency details are important, as the precomputed shading may filter them out [S3].

The claim states that one should not use the technique when high-frequency details are important because precomputed shading filters them out. Source [S3] explicitly states that for diffuse shading (which uses precomputed gradients), the process 'implicitly applies a low pass filter to the gradients... and ignores high-frequency details'. It further notes that this filtering causes rendering artifacts on regular structures. Therefore, the evidence directly supports the claim that precomputed shading filters out high-frequency details.

The claim states that the technique in question (implied to be the one being compared or the proposed method) differs from on-the-fly gradient estimation by 'trading memory for performance'. However, Source [S3] explicitly states that 'On-the-fly gradient estimation trades memory for performance'. The source describes the precomputed method (diffuse shading) as storing gradients in a 3D texture (which implies higher memory usage) but does not characterize the comparison as the precomputed method trading memory for performance relative to on-the-fly estimation; rather, it characterizes on-the-fly estimation as the one that trades memory for performance. Furthermore, the claim attributes the 'low-pass filter' effect to the method storing the result in a 3D texture, which is correct for the precomputed method, but the framing of the trade-off is attributed to the wrong technique in the claim based on the text.

Iterate over the volume grid for $z$ from $1$ to $SLCS-2$, $y$ from $1$ to $ROWS-2$, and $x$ from $1$ to $COLS-2$, skipping boundary layers [S2, unofficial].
